cards.front: Derivative
cards.back: A contract that derives its value from an underlying asset. Options are derivatives; futures are derivatives but are NOT classified as securities. Options are the only derivative securities tested on the SIE.

cards.front: What are the rights and obligations of the buyer vs. the writer of an option?
cards.back: Buyer (long/holder): pays the premium and has the RIGHT to exercise. Risk = premium paid. Writer (short/seller): receives the premium and has the OBLIGATION to perform if exercised.

cards.front: What are the four basic option positions and the market attitude of each?
cards.back: Long call = bullish; Short call = bearish; Long put = bearish; Short put = bullish.

cards.front: What right does the owner of a call hold? What obligation does the writer of a call have?
cards.back: Call owner has the right to BUY 100 shares of the underlying at the strike price before expiration. Call writer has the obligation to SELL 100 shares at the strike price if assigned.

cards.front: What right does the owner of a put hold? What obligation does the writer of a put have?
cards.back: Put owner has the right to SELL 100 shares of the underlying at the strike price before expiration. Put writer has the obligation to BUY 100 shares at the strike price if assigned.

cards.front: In-the-money, At-the-money, Out-of-the-money (Calls)
cards.back: Call is IN the money when stock price > strike. AT the money when stock price = strike. OUT of the money when stock price < strike.

cards.front: In-the-money, At-the-money, Out-of-the-money (Puts)
cards.back: Put is IN the money when stock price < strike. AT the money when stock price = strike. OUT of the money when stock price > strike.

cards.front: Intrinsic Value
cards.back: The amount by which an option is in the money. Always zero or positive—never negative. At-the-money and out-of-the-money options have zero intrinsic value.

cards.front: What is the formula for an option premium, and what two factors affect time value?
cards.back: Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value (IV + TV = Premium). Time value is affected by (1) time to expiration and (2) volatility of the underlying. More time and more volatility = more time value.

cards.front: ABC stock trades at 62. An ABC Jun 60 call trades at a premium of 2. What is the intrinsic value, and is the contract at parity?
cards.back: Intrinsic value = 62 − 60 = 2. Because the premium (2) equals intrinsic value (2), the contract is trading at parity (no time value).

cards.front: Investor is long 1 Jul 40 call at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike + premium = 40 + 3 = 43. MG = unlimited (stock can rise to infinity). ML = premium paid = $300.

cards.front: Investor is short 1 Jul 40 call at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike + premium = 40 + 3 = 43. MG = premium received = $300. ML = unlimited (writer may be forced to buy stock at any price to deliver).

cards.front: Investor is long 1 Jul 40 put at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike − premium = 40 − 3 = 37. MG = strike − premium = 37 points = $3,700 (stock falls to 0). ML = premium paid = $300.

cards.front: Investor is short 1 Jul 40 put at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike − premium = 40 − 3 = 37. MG = premium received = $300. ML = strike − premium = 37 points = $3,700 (stock falls to 0; writer must buy worthless stock at strike).

cards.front: How are index option premiums and exercises calculated, and how do they settle?
cards.back: Index options use a $100 multiplier. Exercise settles in CASH equal to the intrinsic value, delivered the next business day. Settlement price is the closing value on the day of exercise.

What is portfolio insurance using index options, and what type of risk does it hedge?
cards.back: A portfolio manager holding diversified equities buys index puts to offset losses if the market falls. This hedges systematic (market) risk.

cards.front: How do yield-based (interest rate) options work, and what exercise style do they use?
cards.back: Yield-based options move directly with interest rates (strike of 35 = 3.5% yield). Each full point = $1,000. They are European-style exercise—exercisable only on expiration day.

cards.front: EPIC: Which currency options should importers and exporters buy?
cards.back: Exporters buy Puts (concerned foreign currency value will drop). Importers buy Calls (concerned foreign currency value will rise). Foreign currency options are European-style exercise.

cards.front: American-style vs. European-style exercise
cards.back: American-style: may be exercised any time before expiration (nearly all equity and equity index options). European-style: may be exercised ONLY on expiration day (foreign currency options and yield-based options).

cards.front: How does a protective put hedge a long stock position, and what is the breakeven?
cards.back: An investor long stock buys a put to lock in a minimum sale price if the stock declines. Breakeven = stock purchase price + premium paid.

cards.front: How does a protective call hedge a short stock position, and what is the breakeven?
cards.back: An investor short stock buys a call to lock in a maximum repurchase price if the stock rises (controls unlimited risk of short sale). Breakeven = short sale price − premium paid.

cards.front: What is the difference between a covered call and a naked (uncovered) call?
cards.back: Covered call: writer already owns the underlying stock, so delivery is guaranteed—relatively conservative income strategy. Naked call: writer does not own the stock; risk is theoretically unlimited because the stock could rise infinitely before assignment.

cards.front: What is the maximum loss on a naked short put?
cards.back: Strike price − premium received (occurs if the stock falls to zero and the writer is forced to buy worthless stock at the strike). Significant but NOT unlimited.

cards.front: List the steps required to open an options account.
cards.back: (1) RR determines suitability. (2) Customer receives the Options Disclosure Document (ODD) at or before account approval. (3) Account is approved by a Registered Options Principal (ROP). (4) Trading may begin immediately after approval. (5) Signed options agreement must be returned within 15 days of approval—otherwise only closing transactions are permitted.

cards.front: What is the role of the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)?
cards.back: The OCC issues, standardizes, and guarantees the performance of listed options contracts. It sets strike prices, expiration months, and assigns exercise notices to short broker-dealers on a random basis.

cards.front: Listed equity options: trading hours, settlement, expiration, and automatic exercise rule?
cards.back: Trade 9:30 am–4:00 pm ET. Trades settle T+1. Contracts expire third Friday of expiration month at 11:59 pm ET. Any contract in the money by at least $0.01 at expiration is automatically exercised unless 'do not exercise' instructions are given.

cards.front: An investor is long 1 Aug XYZ 30 put when XYZ is trading at 25. What is the intrinsic value/moneyness?
cards.back: The put is IN the money by 5 points (30 strike − 25 market = 5). It has intrinsic value of $500.

cards.front: A customer buys 1 put on Napa Valley Spirits at a strike of $50 with a $4.50 premium. How much did he pay for the contract?
cards.back: $450. Premium of $4.50 × 100 shares = $450. (The strike price is paid only if/when the contract is exercised.)
